Photograph: Zoraida Diaz/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Washington DC Thousands protest closure of the Kennedy Center amid fears Trump is set to demolish the institution Demonstrators gathered outside the building in Washington, after the president was spotted holding a placard that read: ‘Kennedy Center DEMOLIS ...’ David Smith and agencies Fri 18 Sep 2026 23.33 EDT Last modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 04.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google On Friday evening thousands of protesters gathered outside the Kennedy Center in view of the marble facade that remained concealed by scaffolding and tarpaulins, to protest Donald Trump’s plans for the facility and express alarm that he might make good on his threat to tear down the institution. Judge orders Trump administration to give 30 days’ notice before moving to demolish Kennedy Center Read more Crowding streets in the Foggy Bottom area of Washington and locking down traffic as they walked, many carried signs, as they joined in the “Hands Around the Kennedy Center” protest. Some wore costumes and booed when the president was mentioned during the program. Chris Raleigh, co-founder of Hands Off the Arts, which set up the gathering, said in an interview that he hoped the event would show that people are willing to fight to halt Trump’s plans for the building. View image in fullscreen Thousands of demonstrators gather outside the Kennedy Center on Friday. Photograph: Zoraida Diaz/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock One of the most iconic buildings on the Potomac River waterfront, the Kennedy Center has been a focus of Trump’s remake of Washington since 2025, when he began installing favorites on to its governing board. Late last year, he had his name placed on the center. A judge ruled that Trump’s name was illegally added and ordered it removed . The Kennedy Center board, which is aligned with the president, voted Tuesday to close the center indefinitely for repairs hours after US District Judge Christopher Cooper blocked their plans to return Trump’s name to the building. On Thursday, the judge ordered the Kennedy Center to provide 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolishing it. The protests on Friday came after a photo of Trump examining a depiction of the Kennedy Center apparently being demolished sparked widespread attention. In the image captured by AFP photographer Brendan Smialowski on Wednesday, the president was seen through the windows of Air Force One holding a placard with visible text in red declaring: “Kennedy Center DEMOLIS...” The rest of the word was obscured by the plane’s window frame. View image in fullscreen Donald Trump is seen aboard Air Force One checking a Kennedy Center printout. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images Raleigh said he, like others, is concerned Trump could tear down the building without notifying the court. “Look at the East Wing,” he said. “We got up one morning and there was a giant hole there.” Among the demonstrators were people in inflatable animal costumes and a man in a golden Trump mask with a crown and a sign that said: “Restore my name in gold you sycophants.” Another man wore a blue hat that said: “Make America intelligent again.” Baby Trump balloons danced in the air against the setting sun. Protesters beat drums, chanted “hands off!” and waved signs including: “Keep your tiny hands off our Kennedy Center”; “You’re no Jack Kennedy”; “Donny you are no JFK!”; “Kennedy Center 4 ever”; “Our center not DJT’s”; “Hands off the arts”; and “Wicked starring DJT”. View image in fullscreen Drag Queen Tara Hoot holds up signs as she rallies against the closing of the Kennedy Center. Photograph: José Luis Magaña/AP Friday’s event followed a tumultuous week in federal courts in Washington in which filings and counter-filings flooded the courts as the administration continued its push for the president’s vanity projects. The administration has made substantive steps to begin work on a number of projects, despite the fact they are still being litigated. Such projects include Trump’s triumphal arch and the administration’s takeover of East Potomac Golf Links and the US Institute of Peace. Speaking from the Oval Office, Trump said he was willing to save the center, which he said was losing money. He did not address a question about demolishing it. “We have a lot of people working very hard on it to save it,” he said. “I can save it easily, but why should we be doing that and then raise money for the rest of our lives to keep it afloat? Because that’s what you have to do, if we get no recognition. Photograph: RNZAF/RNZAF Official Amelia Earhart Museum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashed Images from New Zealand aerial survey of Nikumaroro in 1938 offer new clues over aviator’s disappearance Oliver Holmes Fri 16 Oct 2026 06.09 EDT Last modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 06.10 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane. The black-and-white images were published by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand after renewed interest in one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century, spurred by a US expedition to the Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro in search of new clues. While some low-resolution copies have been uploaded on blogs, the Air Force Museum of New Zealand said it had received several requests for the photos and had released the full set of 47 images in digital high-resolution format on its website. The negatives were found more than a decade ago by the archivist Matthew O’Sullivan, the keeper of photographs at the museum in Christchurch. View image in fullscreen One of 47 images released by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand of Gardner Island, now Nikumaroro. Photograph: RNZAF/RNZAF Official Earhart’s most prominent investigator, Ric Gillespie, described the images as a “goldmine” in his blog , saying they were a complete set of aerial photos taken on 1 December 1938 by an amphibious biplane during a New Zealand survey of Pacific islands that was looking for suitable airbase locations. What happened to Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan when they disappeared on 2 July 1937 during an attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator has been a stop-and-start search over eight decades, and filled with false leads. A leading theory is that the aviator who broke several records, including becoming the first woman to fly a nonstop solo trip across the Atlantic, ran out of fuel and was marooned on Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island. The hypothesis is that she survived for a while, drinking rainwater and eating fish and turtles, based on signs of a castaway’s campsite and artefacts, including glass from a jar that is thought to have contained cosmetic cream. View image in fullscreen Amelia Earhart standing in front of the Lockheed Electra in which she disappeared in July 1937. Photograph: Alamy This week, archaeologists and scientists from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University in Indianapolis, are searching a part of the island for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape in a lagoon named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image. Other longtime Earhart explorers, including Gillespie, are not convinced, saying it is probably a fallen tree and not the wreckage of her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. The small atoll had been visited dozens of times. In their latest update on Nikumaroro, which is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, the expedition said “severe weather” had hampered their metal-detecting but that they would release an update within 48 hours. “Despite Thursday’s weather delay, the expedition remains on schedule, with two more days of field operations planned – and an update on the identification of the Taraia Object expected,” Purdue University said. “We understand the tremendous interest in what we’re doing at Nikumaroro, and we appreciate everyone’s patience,” said Rick Pettigrew, the expedition lead and executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute. “This is a complex scientific process. You don’t simply arrive at a site and immediately identify what’s there. We have to carefully collect the data, analyse it and reach sound conclusions.” The New Zealand military images are some of the earliest photographic evidence of the island. There is no immediate sign of an object in the Taraia area.
